blocks.title: Stance
blocks.text: During a partition we pick ==availability== over consistency; stale reads are the price, and replicas converge ==eventually==.

items: Every node runs the ==same software== and has the same role
{red:No master}: no leader election, no single point of failure
==Any node== can act as **coordinator** for any key
Coordinator is per request, not per key: the node the client hit
Scale: 100 nodes, ~100 GB each, serving 1M reads/s + 200K writes/s
Coordinator hashes the key and finds its ==N replicas==
Sends to all N at once; does not wait for the slow ones
Replies as soon as ==W== (write) or ==R== (read) replicas answer
Example: N=3, W=2 means the 3rd ack arrives later and is not awaited

items: Replication factor ==N=3==
Replicas spread over **3 availability zones**
One replica per AZ for each key
100 nodes ≈ 33 per AZ

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: No master. ==Any node coordinates==; N=3 replicas in 3 AZs; reply after a **quorum**, not after all.

Many small ranges ==even out load==

blocks.text: Consistent hashing fixes ==data movement==, not ==hot keys==. Use many vnodes per node, and pick replicas on distinct hosts.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Preference list = N **distinct hosts in distinct zones**, not just the next 3 tokens. Writes go to all N in ==parallel== and return after W acks.

items: ==R + W > N== means every read set overlaps the latest successful write set
Standard: {green:N=3, R=2, W=2}, so any 2 replicas read must include 1 that acked the write
Tune R and W per workload to trade read latency against write latency

items: The client picks the level on each `get` and `put`
Mix levels: `QUORUM` writes, `ONE` reads for cheap lookups
Reads and writes must both use quorum levels for R + W > N
R + W > N does {red:not} give ==linearizability==
Concurrent writes can still conflict and need resolution
Sloppy quorums write to stand-in nodes, so a quorum read can miss the latest write
Quorum fails when fewer than R or W replicas respond
==Stale-read rate== per consistency level
==Quorum failure rate== (requests unable to reach R or W)
==p99 latency== per level: targets read under 10 ms, write under 15 ms

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Overlap gives the newest ==acked== write a chance to be seen, not a guarantee. N=3, R=2, W=2 is a tuning default, not strong consistency.

sections.title: Conflict Resolution: Vector Clocks vs LWW

pages.title: Conflict Resolution: Vector Clocks vs LWW

items: A ==vector clock== is a list of **(node, counter)** pairs attached to each version
Version A ==descends== B if **every** counter in A is ≥ B's
If neither version descends the other, they are {orange:concurrent}
Concurrent versions are kept as ==siblings== and returned to the client to merge
D3 lacks the C counter and D4 lacks the B counter, so neither descends
D3 and D4 {red:conflict}: a get returns **both** siblings
The client merges them and writes back with a clock that descends both
LWW: clock skew of even ==100 ms== silently drops a legitimate write
Vector clock: size grows with writers, so truncate at ~==10 entries==
Vector clock: the app must merge, e.g. shopping cart = **union** of siblings
Do not use LWW where a lost write is unacceptable; use vector clocks or CRDTs

blocks.title: Pick by cost of a lost write
blocks.text: Idempotent overwrite (a profile photo URL): ==LWW==. A write you cannot lose (a cart): **vector clocks** or CRDTs.
Running example: Dynamo-style Distributed Key-Value Store, N=3, W=2, 200K writes/s over 100 nodes.

items: ==Hinted handoff== keeps writes **available** while a preference-list replica is temporarily down
Preference list for key k: {blue:A}, {blue:B}, {blue:C}; B is down
{green:Sloppy quorum}: write goes to the first N ==healthy== nodes on the ring
So node D (next clockwise) stands in for B and the W=2 acks still arrive

rows: Reads may miss the new copy

nodes.sub: D sends hint to B, deletes it

items: The hint is stored apart from D's own data, so D does not serve it as its replica
D deletes the hint only after B **acks** the replay
One row per missed write: ==target node==, key, value, version, `created_at`
Rows expire after a ==TTL of ~3 hours==, which bounds disk use on the stand-in

blocks.note: replay scans by target_node when it comes back UP

items: Stand-in D dies before replay: the hint is lost, B stays stale
Owner down longer than ~3 h: the hint expires, B stays stale
Only ==anti-entropy== (Merkle trees) repairs that replica afterwards

Hints replayed per second

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Hinted handoff is a ==short-outage== patch for availability. It is not durability: a lost or expired hint needs **anti-entropy**.
Background repair of replica divergence in the Distributed KV Store (100 nodes, ~100 GB each, N=3).

spec.title: Two replicas of one token range

items: ==One tree per token range== per node (with N=3 and vnodes, a node holds many trees)
~==64K leaves== (65,536) per tree, so ~16 levels deep
Trees are ==rebuilt periodically==, not updated per write
Replicas must build trees over the same range with the same leaf boundaries
Schedule: Merkle repair ==weekly== per range
Tree rebuild is ==I/O heavy==: it reads every key in the range; throttle and stagger
Rebalance (join/leave) changes range membership and ==invalidates trees==; rebuild
Leaf too coarse: one stale key streams the whole ~1.5 MB leaf

Bytes streamed per repair
Ranges not repaired in over {red:10 days}: alert
10 days = tombstone GC grace period, so stay under it

blocks.title: Repair or resurrect
blocks.text: If a range goes unrepaired past ==gc_grace (10 days)==, a replica that missed a delete can bring the **deleted data back**. Repair weekly.

items: {green:Decentralized} membership and liveness: ==no central coordinator==
Every node learns who is alive from its peers, never from a master
Every **1 s** each node exchanges state with ==1-3 random peers==
Information reaches all N nodes in ==O(log N)== rounds
100 nodes: about 7 rounds, so roughly 7 s to converge

Status and token changes ride along in the same gossip

blocks.title: Seed nodes
items: New member contacts a seed first to learn the ring
Everyone gossips with seeds, so ==no split gossip clusters==
Seeds are only a contact point, not a coordinator
Network partition: ==both sides mark the other DOWN==
False positive DOWN triggers **needless hinted handoff**
Nodes marked DOWN then UP repeatedly are ==flapping==

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text: Gossip spreads state in **O(log N)** rounds; a node goes DOWN at ==phi above 8==, and a false positive only costs extra hints.
Per-replica storage in the Distributed KV Store: 200K writes/s x N=3 over 100 nodes is ~6K local writes/s per node, all durable.

items: Job: make local writes ==fast== and ==durable== on each replica
The commit log is ==append-only==, so the disk does sequential writes, no seeks
Ack after the log append and the memtable insert, never after a flush
Flush writes the memtable as an {purple:immutable sorted SSTable}; a new memtable takes over
Bloom filter says ==definitely absent== or ==maybe present==
~1% false positives; it never gives a false negative
A skipped file costs no disk read, so most SSTables are never opened
Compaction ==merges SSTables== into fewer, larger sorted files
Drops {red:overwritten values} and {red:expired tombstones}
Fewer files means fewer files to check on each read
A delete writes a ==tombstone== marker, not an in-place removal

blocks.title: Rules
items: Crash recovery: ==replay the commit log== to rebuild the memtable
Keep tombstones for ==gc_grace = 10 days==
Run repair on every range within gc_grace

blocks.title: Zombie data
blocks.text: If a tombstone is purged before a down replica gets it, that replica still holds the old value and ==the deleted data resurrects==.

**Add a node without a reshuffle?** ==Consistent hashing + vnodes==: only ~1/N of keys move

blocks.title: Cheatsheet
items: Ring via Murmur3, 2^128 space
Gossip every 1 s, phi above 8 = DOWN
Hints kept ~3 h
Merkle repair weekly

blocks.q: N=3 and a QUORUM write needs W=2. Two of the three preference-list replicas are down. What happens, and what changes with a sloppy quorum?
a_bullets: Strict quorum: only 1 ack is possible, so the write ==fails== (or times out).
Sloppy quorum: the write goes to the next healthy nodes on the ring, with hints naming the real owners, so it ==succeeds==.
The cost: those stand-ins are not in the preference list, so R + W > N no longer guarantees a read sees this write.
Consistency level ONE would also succeed, because one ack is enough.

blocks.q: A team sets N=3, R=1, W=2 and expects every read to return the latest acknowledged write. Is that right?
a_bullets: No. R + W = 3, which is not greater than N = 3, so a read and a write quorum can miss each other.
The write may be acked by replicas 1 and 2 while replica 3 still holds the old value.
An R=1 read can hit replica 3 and return stale data.
Fix: raise to R=2 (R + W = 4 > 3) or to W=3.
Even with R + W > N, concurrent writes and sloppy quorums can still return stale data, so this is not linearizability.

blocks.q: Version D3 has clock [(A,2),(B,1)] and D4 has [(A,2),(C,1)]. Which one wins, and what does the client see?
a_bullets: Neither wins. D4 has no B counter, so it does not descend D3. D3 has no C counter, so it does not descend D4.
They are ==concurrent==, so the store keeps both as siblings and returns both on a read.
The client merges them (for example a cart union) and writes back through A.
The new clock [(A,3),(B,1),(C,1)] is at least as large as both on every counter, so it descends both and replaces them.
Last-write-wins would instead keep the higher timestamp and silently drop the other write.

blocks.q: A cluster grows from 10 to 11 nodes. Roughly what fraction of keys moves under hash(key) mod N, and under consistent hashing?
a_bullets: Mod N: about (N-1)/N, so roughly 10/11, or ~91% of keys, change owner. That is a near-total reshuffle.
Consistent hashing: about 1/N, so roughly 1/11, or ~9%. Only the ranges the new node takes over move.
With vnodes the new node takes many small token ranges from many neighbors.
That spreads the streaming load and keeps the load even, with no downtime.

blocks.q: A node is down for 12 days. The cluster uses gc_grace = 10 days and nobody ran repair. After the node returns, a key deleted on day 1 reappears. Why?
a_bullets: The delete wrote a tombstone to the live replicas. Compaction dropped it after 10 days.
The returning node still holds the old live value, and no replica holds a tombstone to override it.
Anti-entropy now sees a difference and copies the old value to the other replicas, so the ==deleted data resurrects==.
Fix: run repair within gc_grace, and rebuild any node that was down longer than gc_grace instead of letting it rejoin as is.
Hints do not help here: they expire after ~3 hours, far shorter than 12 days.
